newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Royal Caribbean sees sales gains.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Royal Caribbean sees sales gains.

text.p: Sales growth rather than cost cuts will drive earnings higher at Royal Caribbean International after a $1.3 billion acquisition of upmarket cruise operator Celebrity Cruise Lines Inc, Royal's chief executive said on Tuesday.
"The most powerful force will be on revenue. Even a small rise in revenues translates into a big gain on the bottom line," Richard Fain told Reuters.

Earlier Tuesday, Royal Caribbean, the No. 2 cruise-ship company after Carnival Inc, said it agreed to buy Celebrity for $1.3 billion in cash, Royal Caribbean shares and assumption of about $800 million in debt.
Celebrity, owned by Overseas Shipbuilding Group Inc and Chandris Group, operates four recently built cruise ships. It is scheduled to take delivery in October of still another new ship, the Mercury.
Altogether, the deal adds 8,200 berths to Royal Caribbean's 19,770. Royal Caribbean now has 11 ships and has contracted for two more enormous, 130,000-ton ships, due in 1999 and later.
Analysts applauded the deal, saying Royal Caribbean was paying close to book value for Celebrity, or about what it would cost to replace the five Celebrity vessels.
New ships, which are typically larger and decked out with features such as waterslides and nine-story atriums, are increasingly important for attracting mass-market cruise passengers, analysts said.
"Hardware and on-board amenties are very important," said analyst Scott Barry of Raymond James. "The core cruise-vacation markets are being dominated by the new tonnage."
Fain said Royal may redeploy some of the Celebrity ships.
"There are some opportunities to make more efficient use of the ships," Fain said. "I would expect it will ease our entree into Europe."

U.S. cruise operators such as Carnival and Royal Caribbean are increasingly moving overseas into the comparatively small but highly promising markets of Asia and Europe. Carnival just completed an acquisition of Italian operator, Costa.
Celebrity now sails mainly to Caribbean ports, as does Royal Caribbean, but also is active in Alaska.

Fain said the combination gives Royal Caribbean another well-known cruise-ship brand, one with minimal overlap with its own primarily mid-market offerings, and another line of trips to offer through its large salesforce.
Celebrity is a so-called premium operator, charging higher prices than many other cruise companies for holidays a week or longer. It's profitability has been weak, analysts said.
"Celebrity has an outstanding product and reputation, but it hasn't been large enough by itself to take full advantage of those things," Fain said. "We give them scale and size."
Fain said the deal, which involves 7.4 million new Royal Caribbean shares, would dilute earnings per share in 1998, but would benefit EPS beginning in 1999. He declined to estimate the dilution.
